rationale: Scanner and protocol differences across the 8 ADHD-200 sites cause big shifts in connectivity values. Since the score is AUROC within each site, I'll z-score each connectivity feature within each site, using train and test subjects of that site pooled together (no labels involved). This removes the between-site variance, so the low-capacity L2 logistic model can spend its budget on the within-site ADHD signal instead.

Scanner and protocol differences between ADHD-200 sites are large, and the metric is AUROC within each site. Site effects probably take up a lot of the variance in the logistic regression's connectivity features. To remove them, each feature is standardised separately within each site before the classifier sees it. This is a ComBat-style location/scale harmonisation. It uses only feature values, never labels. Each site's statistics come from all of that site's items in the current fit, train and test together, so the scaling also uses test items' features. The regression can then learn within-site ADHD differences instead of between-site offsets.

I'm z-scoring every connectivity feature within each acquisition site before the global scaler and logistic regression. Scanner and protocol differences between the 8 ADHD-200 sites are large, but the score only compares subjects within a site. Removing per-site offsets and scales should stop the model spending its capacity on site differences and leave the diagnosis signal. Site is used only for this harmonization step, never as a predictor.

Switch from raw Pearson correlations to a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk covariance matrices. The reference mean is fit on the training fold only. This is the most consistently strong FC representation in benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019). Shrinkage matters here because many ADHD-200 sites have short scans relative to 200 ROIs. The tangent projection also whitens away the shared group-level connectivity structure, which can reduce site-driven variance.

The 8 ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner and protocol, which shifts the connectivity values at each site. Because scoring is within site, those site-level offsets only add noise to the classifier. This change z-scores every connectivity feature within each site (label-free, using that site's train and test subjects together) before the L2 logistic regression, so the model learns case-vs-control patterns that are shared across sites.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner and protocol, so the site shifts in connectivity are probably much larger than the ADHD effect. The score is within-site AUROC, so I am z-scoring every connectivity feature within each site (mean and SD taken from that site's subjects, no labels used) before the L2 logistic regression. This removes site offsets and scale differences, so the classifier is fit on differences between subjects inside the same site.

The scanner and protocol differences between ADHD-200 sites are large, and they probably dominate the connectivity features. The pooled logistic regression can end up spending capacity on site offsets that don't help within-site AUROC. So the one change is to z-score each connectivity feature within its acquisition site before fitting. Test subjects use their site's training statistics, and the test batch's own (label-free) statistics if the site has few training subjects. This is a simple, label-free harmonization that only uses site metadata.

I'm replacing Fisher-z Pearson features with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariances on CC200, keeping the classifier the same. Large connectome benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019) found tangent space was the most reliable connectivity measure for multi-site rs-fMRI classification. It should also help with ADHD-200's short scans: shrinkage stabilises the ~190×190 estimates, and whitening by a group reference matrix removes structure every subject shares.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, TR and number of timepoints. Those differences shift the connectivity features by site and can swamp the weak ADHD signal. This change centres and scales each connectivity edge within each site before the logistic regression. The site statistics are computed without labels, from the training and test subjects of that site together. Site is used only for this harmonization, never as a predictor, so the model has to separate cases from controls within each site. That is also how the metric scores it.

I'm switching from Pearson z-correlations to a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk correlation matrices, taken around the log-Euclidean mean of all subjects. Many ADHD-200 scans are short, so 200-ROI correlation estimates are noisy. Shrinkage stabilizes them, and the tangent space gives a geometry where linear models do well. Benchmarks (e.g. Dadi et al. 2019) found tangent space the most reliable connectivity measure for linear classifiers on rs-fMRI. The classifier stays the same.

Scanner and protocol differences between the 8 ADHD-200 sites shift the connectivity features a lot. Because scoring is within-site AUROC, the classifier wastes capacity on between-site variation. I'm z-scoring each connectivity edge within each site (a simple location/scale harmonization in the ComBat style) before the L2 logistic regression, so the model only learns contrasts within a site. This uses no labels: test-site statistics come from the training items of that site, and fall back to the test items themselves if a site never appears in training.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, protocol and ADHD prevalence. A single global model can therefore learn connectivity patterns that only mark the site, which does nothing for within-site AUROC. I will remove each site's mean and scale from every connectivity edge, so the classifier has to learn from within-site differences between ADHD and control subjects.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, protocol, TR and scan length, and those differences shift connectivity values much more than ADHD does. A single linear model fit across sites therefore spends its capacity on site offsets, which can't help a within-site AUROC. This version z-scores every connectivity feature within each site before the L2 logistic regression. The site statistics come from that site's training subjects (label-free), so only the within-site differences that the metric scores are left.

In ADHD-200, scanner and protocol differences between sites are much larger than any ADHD effect. Because sites also differ in how many ADHD cases they have, the logistic model can learn site offsets as a stand-in for diagnosis. This change z-scores each connectivity feature within its own site (using that site's training-set statistics; no labels are used) before the global scaler, to remove that confound and leave the within-site differences that the metric scores.

Scanner and protocol differences between sites probably account for much of the variance in the connectivity features. The metric only compares subjects within the same site, so this change z-scores each connectivity edge within each site before fitting the L2 logistic regression. Site statistics come from that site's train and test features combined, which uses no labels, so the classifier should learn differences within a site rather than scanner offsets.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, protocol and ADHD prevalence. With unharmonized features, the L2 logistic regression partly learns which site a subject comes from, and that is useless for within-site AUROC. This change z-scores each connectivity edge within each site (using training-fold statistics for that site, or the test subjects' own label-free statistics if the site is new) before the global scaler and classifier. The goal is for the model to learn only within-site differences in connectivity between cases and controls.

Scoring is within-site and scanner/protocol differences between sites are large, so I'm z-scoring each connectivity feature within its site (ComBat-lite, label-free). That takes site offsets and scale differences out of the training signal, so the regularized logistic model learns ADHD-vs-control differences that hold inside a site rather than spending its weights on site variance.

ADHD-200 has large scanner and protocol differences between sites, and the score is AUROC computed within each site, so between-site offsets in connectivity only add noise for the classifier. This change z-scores each connectivity feature within its acquisition site. It uses site only to harmonize features, never as a predictor, and estimates the scaling from training subjects of that site where available. It also loads the `athena` strategy explicitly instead of falling back to it.

Scanner and protocol differences between sites are large, and the metric only compares subjects within the same site. So site offsets in the connectivity features are nuisance variance that the L2 logistic model has to fit around. I'm adding per-site z-scoring of the Fisher-z connectivity features before the shared logistic regression. Statistics come from the training items of each site; if a test site has no training items, the test items' own label-free statistics are used. This lets the classifier learn diagnosis-related connectivity differences instead of site signatures.

I'm replacing raw Pearson correlations with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk connectivity matrices. Benchmarks on ABIDE/ADHD-200 (Dadi et al. 2019) found this connectivity measure the most reliable for diagnosis. It also accounts for the geometry of SPD matrices and stabilises estimates from the short, site-dependent scan lengths. The reference mean is fit only on the training fold, so nothing leaks from test subjects.
